title: Guwahati Mom, 62, Turned Her Love for Sweets Into a Rs 2.5 Lakh-a-Month Business
excerpt: Sunita Agarwal started Kitchen & Gupshup from her home kitchen in 2022 with four items; today it serves nearly 3,000 customers — and she is helping other women earn from home too.
body:
• At 62, Guwahati homemaker Sunita Agarwal turned her lifelong love of making sweets into Kitchen & Gupshup, a business that now earns Rs 2–2.5 lakh a month and serves nearly 3,000 customers.
  • Started in 2022 as a home kitchen with four items — besan barfi, gond barfi, masala channa daal and mathris — the venture grew to 30+ SKUs by 2024 and now runs from a commercial kitchen.
  • Her pitch: handmade sweets with pure ghee and no artificial flavours, recipes perfected over decades of cooking for her own family.
  • Sunita is extending the model to other women — two sellers from Shillong and Assam already earn 23% of their sales working from home, with no targets or fixed hours — and the family plans to enter quick commerce next.

At 62, Sunita Agarwal of Guwahati has done what many home cooks only joke about: she turned her kitchen into a business. Kitchen & Gupshup, the sweets and savouries venture she started from her home kitchen in 2022 with just four items, now serves nearly 3,000 customers and brings in Rs 2–2.5 lakh a month, according to The Better India, which first reported her story.

"Since childhood, I was always fond of making sweets and snacks," Sunita says. For years she cooked for her children, often dissatisfied with the quality of store-bought sweets. "So I started making it for them," she says. As her children grew older, the food she shared with friends and family kept drawing the same reaction — that taste you no longer find in the market. The thought that followed was simple: "Why not make this a business?"

From four items to a commercial kitchen

Kitchen & Gupshup began with four homemade favourites: besan barfi, gond barfi, masala channa daal and mathris. The first year was Guwahati-only, building confidence one batch at a time. Around then her son Rajvardhan, who had left his job and was deciding what to do next, joined her. "I left my job, and we were figuring out what was to be done. That's when my mom said, 'Let's make this bigger,'" he recalls.

Rajvardhan travelled across northern and western India studying the traditional sweets ecosystem and recruiting halwais — professional sweet makers — from Rajasthan and Haryana. By 2024 the venture had expanded to more than 30 SKUs across sweet and savoury and moved into a commercial kitchen with standard food-safety practices. Today the team is eight strong: four in operations and marketing, four in the kitchen. Sunita still tastes and approves every batch before it is packed. "Our motive is to ensure customer satisfaction," she says.

The differentiator: hands, ghee, no shortcuts

The family's positioning is deliberately old-fashioned. "My mom was different from many of them," Rajvardhan says. "My mom makes with hands, pure ghee, no artificial flavours." Traditional recipes sit at the centre while the team experiments with fusion products for modern palates. In 2026, after a year of steady city sales, K&G expanded beyond Guwahati through its own website and Amazon, and the family is planning to enter quick commerce — a channel that could materially change a business built on perishable, made-to-order sweets.

Beyond one kitchen: women earning from home

The numbers are modest but directionally significant: nearly 3,000 customers, four to five orders a day, Rs 2–2.5 lakh in monthly revenue, with a target of Rs 6–7 lakh. A B2B corporate-gifting line adds another channel. More unusual is what Sunita is doing with the model itself. Having built a business later in life, she is onboarding other women as home-based sellers — she supplies the products, they find customers and keep 23 percent of their sales, with training and no targets or fixed hours.

"I always felt women need a platform to be financially independent, and I wanted to give them that platform."

— Sunita Agarwal, founder, Kitchen & Gupshup

Two women from Shillong and Assam have joined so far. One, Prem Agarwal of Shillong, is both her family's breadwinner and her unwell husband's caregiver; she earns Rs 6,000–7,000 a month from home through the initiative. "From home I work. I just need to get orders for them, and then they will take care of everything," she says.

A familiar dream for the diaspora

For the diaspora, Sunita's story lands on familiar ground: the home-kitchen-to-D2C arc is one many NRI food entrepreneurs have walked, and regional Indian sweets remain among the most ordered categories when the diaspora shops for a taste of home. Her model — recipes as intellectual property, quality as the moat — travels well.

What's next

The family's immediate plans are scale: quick commerce, the Rs 6–7 lakh monthly revenue target, and a wider network of women sellers. Sunita herself remains the quality control department — planning every order, checking every sweet. Years after asking herself why not make it a business, she is still in the kitchen, working with recipes she perfected making for her family, now as the owner of something she can call her own.
image_caption: An older woman in a sari prepares sweets by hand in a commercial kitchen, with trays of savouries and her team around her. Sunita Agarwal started Kitchen & Gupshup from her Guwahati home kitchen in 2022; the business now serves nearly 3,000 customers.
nri_angle: For the diaspora, Sunita's story captures how the flavours of home — and the women who carry them — are becoming serious businesses back in India.
author: Diaspora Desk
